Vector space (V)

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Algebra Linear algebra
OurBigBook.com Words: 13k Articles: 234
A vector space over a field F is a set V equipped with vector addition and scalar multiplication satisfying the vector space axioms. Its vectors can represent directed displacements, lists of measurements, polynomials, or entire functions. The common structure is that adding two elements and multiplying an element by a scalar remain meaningful operations inside the same space.
For example, R2 uses coordinatewise addition and scaling. With
b1​=(2,1),b2​=(1,2),v=(5,4),
(1)
we have v=2b1​+b2​. Moving twice along b1​ and once along b2​ reaches the same vector as five horizontal and four vertical steps. The two descriptions refer to different bases of the same space. A basis makes such descriptions unique; a spanning set makes them possible.
The space R[x]≤2​ of real polynomials of degree at most two has basis 1,x,x2: the polynomial 3−2x+x2 is the linear combination with coordinates (3,−2,1). The zero vector here is the zero polynomial, and addition combines coefficients. A derivative is a linear map on this space; its matrix records how it acts on the three basis vectors. The same coordinate machinery therefore handles both geometric motion and operations on functions.
The choice of field matters. The complex numbers form a one-dimensional vector space over C with basis 1, but a two-dimensional vector space over R with basis 1,i. The question "how many independent directions?" has an answer only after the allowed scalars are specified. Likewise, polynomials of degree exactly two do not form a vector space: subtraction can remove the leading term, and the zero polynomial is absent.
The usefulness of the abstraction is that a linear map is determined by its values on a basis. Once those images are known, linear combinations give its action on every vector. The rank-nullity theorem relates the number of attainable outputs to the number of invisible input directions, while change of basis lets us choose coordinates suited to the problem. Eigenvectors, for example, choose directions on which repeated application of a linear operator becomes scalar multiplication.
A historical source is Hermann Grassmann's Die lineale Ausdehnungslehre (1844). Its full title advertises applications to other branches of mathematics, statics, mechanics, magnetism and crystallography; the original edition is digitized by ETH-Bibliothek. This gives an early setting for treating geometric quantities algebraically across different applications, rather than attributing the modern axiom list to that title alone.[ref]

Complexification of a real vector space (VC​=V⊗R​C)

Words: 96
Vector space OurBigBook.com
The complexification of a real vector space V allows complex scalar coefficients while preserving its real linear relations. It can be constructed as the tensor product V⊗R​C, or as formal sums u+iv with u,v∈V. A real basis of V becomes a complex basis of VC​, so its complex dimension equals the original real dimension. Every real linear map extends uniquely by complex linearity. In particular a real representation extends by viewing its real matrices as complex matrices. Complexifying the realification of a complex representation produces the original complex representation together with its complex conjugate; the coordinate change (u,v)↦(u+iv,u−iv) exhibits the two blocks.

Vector space axioms

Words: 55
Vector space OurBigBook.com
Addition makes V an Abelian group: for all u,v,w∈V, (u+v)+w=u+(v+w) and u+v=v+u, there is a zero vector 0, and every v has an additive inverse −v. Scalar multiplication satisfies, for a,b∈F,
1v=v,(ab)v=a(bv),a(u+v)=au+av,(a+b)v=av+bv.
(2)
Both operations take values in V. These requirements make manipulating linear combinations independent of how sums are grouped or expanded.

Sequence space

Words: 25
Vector space OurBigBook.com
A sequence space is a vector space of scalar sequences, closed under coordinatewise addition and scalar multiplication. Examples include the l-p sequence space, the l-infinity sequence space and spaces of convergent sequences.

Zero vector (0)

Words: 42
Vector space OurBigBook.com
The zero vector of a vector space is its additive identity: v+0=0+v=v for every vector v. It is unique, because if 0′ is another such identity then 0=0+0′=0′. Distributivity gives α0=α(0+0)=α0+α0, so α0=0 after cancellation. In a coordinate vector space it has every coordinate zero.

Vector space over the rational numbers (V over Q)

Words: 25
Vector space OurBigBook.com
A vector space with scalar field Q is equivalently a torsion-free divisible Abelian group. An embedding of such groups automatically respects rational scalar multiplication because solutions to nb=ma are unique.

Antilinear map

Words: 146 Articles: 2
Vector space OurBigBook.com
For complex vector spaces, an antilinear map satisfies A(αu+βv)=αAu+β​Av. It is linear over the real numbers and conjugates complex scalar multiplication. This differs from two conjugate linear operators, which are related by similarity rather than conjugate-linearity.

Quaternionic structure on a complex vector space (J2=−1)

Words: 67
Antilinear map OurBigBook.com
An antilinear endomorphism J with square −1 equips a complex vector space with a quaternionic structure: complex multiplication supplies the quaternionic generator i and J supplies j, satisfying Ji=−iJ. Such a space has even complex dimension. There is no invariant complex line, because Jv=cv would imply −v=∣c∣2v. In dimension four the invariant complex two-planes are quaternionic lines, forming HP1≅S4. This is the Euclidean reality structure on twistor space used in twistor theory.

Antiunitary operator (⟨Au,Av⟩=⟨u,v⟩​)

Words: 44
Antilinear map OurBigBook.com
An antiunitary operator between complex Hilbert spaces is a surjective antilinear map satisfying the displayed inner product identity. It preserves norms but conjugates scalars. In a chosen orthonormal basis it is UK, with U a unitary operator and K coefficientwise complex conjugation. Conversely any such UK is antiunitary. Antilinearity by itself does not preserve norms.

A vector space over the field of complex numbers. A complex-linear map preserves addition and multiplication by complex scalars.

A real vector space is a vector space over the field R of real numbers.

Majorization (x≺y)

Words: 203 Articles: 2
Real vector space OurBigBook.com
For real vectors of equal length and equal sum, write x≺y when ∑j=1k​xj↓​≤∑j=1k​yj↓​ for every proper initial segment; the downward arrow means decreasing rearrangement. Majorization compares how unevenly a fixed total is distributed. The uniform probability vector is majorized by every probability vector, while (1,0,…,0) majorizes every probability vector. The order controls exact pure-state entanglement conversion in Nielsen's pure-state conversion theorem.

Majorization of summable sequences (x≺y)

Words: 142 Articles: 1
Majorization OurBigBook.com
For decreasing positive sequences in ℓ1, write x≺y if every initial partial sum of x is at most the corresponding partial sum of y and the finite total sums agree. The finiteness requirement matters: equality of two divergent totals interpreted as infinity is too weak to guarantee a doubly stochastic realization of summable-sequence majorization.
Doubly stochastic realization of summable-sequence majorization (xi​=∑j​pij​yj​)
Words: 95
Majorization of summable sequences OurBigBook.com
Decreasing strictly positive summable sequences with equal totals and x≺y admit an infinite doubly stochastic matrix realizing the displayed relation. Choose k with yk​≥x1​>yk+1​ and average the pair to obtain x1​ and yk​+yk+1​−x1​. The remaining decreasing sequence majorizes the remaining target sequence: short initial sums contain values at least x1​, and longer sums are the old sums minus x1​. Repeat on the tail, freezing one normalized finite-support row at each stage. Limit column sums are at most one; Tonelli's theorem, equal finite totals and strict positivity of every yj​ force every column sum to equal one.

Vector space over a finite field

Words: 205 Articles: 3
Vector space OurBigBook.com
If Fq​ is a finite field, a vector space of finite dimension d over Fq​ has qd elements. Every infinite-dimensional vector space over Fp​ is an infinite elementary abelian p-group under addition.

Finite-field Kakeya set

Words: 169 Articles: 2
Vector space over a finite field OurBigBook.com
A subset of Fqn​ is a finite-field Kakeya set when it contains an affine line in a vector space in every one-dimensional direction. The line position may depend on the direction. The polynomial method in combinatorics yields the finite-field Kakeya polynomial bound on its cardinality.

Tangent-line finite-field Kakeya construction (K={(x,y):x2−y is a square}∪{x=0})

Words: 62
Finite-field Kakeya set OurBigBook.com
For odd characteristic, the union of the lines y=mx−m2/4 contains a line of every finite slope. For fixed x, completing the square shows that it comprises the (p+1)/2 values of y for which x2−y is a square, including zero. Adding the vertical line x=0 completes the directions and gives cardinality (p2+2p−1)/2=(1/2+o(1))p2. This is a finite-field Kakeya set whose density tends to one half.

Finite-field Kakeya polynomial bound (∣A∣≥(nq+n−1​)≥qn/n!)

Words: 75
Finite-field Kakeya set OurBigBook.com
For a finite-field Kakeya set A⊆Fqn​, a smaller cardinality would give a nonzero polynomial of total degree of a polynomial at most q−1 vanishing on A, by the dimension of a bounded-total-degree polynomial space. Its restriction to each complete affine line in a vector space has q roots of a polynomial and degree less than q, hence vanishes identically. The top homogeneous polynomial part then vanishes in every direction. A polynomial of degree less than q in each variable cannot vanish everywhere on Fqn​ unless it is zero, giving a contradiction. For the prime field, this is the polynomial nonvanishing below the field size.

Linear span (span(S))

Words: 168 Articles: 2
Vector space OurBigBook.com
The linear span of a subset S of a vector space is the set of all finite linear combinations of elements of S. It is the smallest vector subspace containing S: every vector subspace containing the original vectors must contain their sums and scalar multiples.
In R3, the linear span of (1,0,0) is a line, the linear span of (1,0,0),(0,1,0) is the plane z=0, and adding (0,0,1) gives all of R3. Adding (2,0,0) to the first set changes none of its attainable vectors, because it is already a scalar multiple of (1,0,0). Thus a spanning set can contain redundant generators; linear independence identifies when this redundancy is absent. In an infinite-dimensional space, an algebraic linear span still uses finite sums; a closed linear span can also include limits in a specified norm.

Closed linear span (span​S)

Words: 39
Linear span OurBigBook.com
In a normed vector space, the closed linear span of S is the closure of its linear span in the norm topology. It includes limits of finite linear combinations. In a Hilbert space, an infinite orthonormal basis spans in this closed sense, allowing norm-convergent series in addition to finite sums.

Spanning set

Words: 16
Linear span OurBigBook.com
A subset S of a vector space is a spanning set when its linear span is the whole vector space.

Quotient vector space (V/W)

Words: 86 Articles: 1
Vector space OurBigBook.com
For a vector subspace W≤V, the quotient vector space V/W consists of cosets v+W, with vector operations induced from V.

Parallel lines as a quotient vector space (R3/span(u))

Words: 64
Quotient vector space OurBigBook.com
For fixed u=0, the parallel affine lines lx​=x+span(u) are precisely the cosets of the indicated quotient vector space. Changing representatives adds a multiple of u, so lx​+ly​=lx+y​ and alx​=lax​ are well-defined. The zero is the whole line l0​, not a single point. If (u,b1​,b2​) is a basis, the two line classes lb1​​,lb2​​ form a basis of the quotient by spanning and independence modulo span(u).

Vector subspace

Words: 448 Articles: 9
Vector space OurBigBook.com
A vector subspace is a nonempty subset of a vector space closed under vector addition and scalar multiplication, and is therefore itself a vector space. Equivalently, whenever u,v belong to the subset, so does au+bv for all allowed scalars a,b. In particular it contains the zero vector.
For example, the plane W={(x,y,z):x+y+z=0}⊆R3 is a vector subspace, with basis (1,−1,0),(1,0,−1). Indeed every element is (−y)(1,−1,0)+(−z)(1,0,−1). The parallel plane x+y+z=1 misses the zero vector and is an affine subspace instead. Homogeneous constraints produce vector subspaces: W is the kernel of the linear map (x,y,z)↦x+y+z. This lets us describe all solutions of a homogeneous linear equation through a basis of its kernel.

Proper vector subspace (U⊊V)

Words: 45
Vector subspace OurBigBook.com
A proper vector subspace of a vector space is one strictly smaller than the ambient space. In a finite-dimensional vector space, this is equivalent to having smaller dimension: a basis of the subspace can be extended to a basis of the ambient space, and strict inclusion requires at least one additional vector.

Flag (linear algebra, 0=V0​⊂V1​⊂⋯⊂Vr​=V)

Words: 99 Articles: 1
Vector subspace OurBigBook.com
A flag is a strictly nested chain of vector subspaces of a fixed vector space. A complete flag contains a subspace of every possible dimension. For an action by linear maps, an invariant flag means that each of its vector subspaces is an invariant subspace. A basis adapted to an invariant complete flag makes all these maps upper triangular, connecting complete flags to simultaneous triangularization of a Lie algebra representation.

Complete flag (0=V0​⊂V1​⊂⋯⊂Vn​=V)

Words: 47
Flag (linear algebra) OurBigBook.com
A complete flag in an n-dimensional vector space is a nested sequence of vector subspaces with dimVi​=i. An action preserves such a flag exactly when its matrices are upper triangular in a basis adapted to the flag. The Lie theorem supplies an invariant complete flag for every complex finite-dimensional Lie algebra representation of a solvable Lie algebra.

Fixed coordinate subspace (Rkp​={θ:θj​=0 (j>k)})

Words: 47
Vector subspace OurBigBook.com
The fixed coordinate subspace of dimension k in Rp consists of vectors whose coordinates after the first k vanish. Restricting a quadratic form to it uses only the leading k by k matrix block. It specifies one fixed support; allowing every support of size k would introduce another combinatorial counting step.

Intersection of vector subspaces (U∩W)

Words: 27
Vector subspace OurBigBook.com
The intersection of any family of vector subspaces of a common vector space is the set of vectors belonging to every member of the family. It is again a vector subspace.

Sum of vector subspaces (U+W)

Vector subspace OurBigBook.com
The sum of vector subspaces U,W≤V is
U+W={u+w:u∈U, w∈W}.
(3)
It is the smallest vector subspace containing both U and W.

Hyperplane

Words: 23
Vector subspace OurBigBook.com
A hyperplane is a vector subspace of codimension one. A projective hyperplane in Pn is the zero set of one nonzero homogeneous linear form.

Closed vector subspace

Words: 91 Articles: 1
Vector subspace OurBigBook.com
A closed vector subspace of a topological vector space is both a vector subspace and a closed set. The kernel of a continuous linear map is a closed vector subspace.

Positive distance between a unit sphere and a disjoint finite-dimensional subspace (dist(SE​,F)>0)

Words: 70
Closed vector subspace OurBigBook.com
If E is a nonzero closed linear subspace of a normed ambient space and F is finite-dimensional with E∩F={0}, the unit sphere of E has positive distance from F. Otherwise a sequence of nearly coincident points yields a bounded sequence in F, hence a convergent subsequence; closedness of E puts its norm-one limit in both vector subspaces. In applications to a bidual space, completeness of the Banach space makes its canonical image closed.

Affine subspace

Words: 211 Articles: 3
Vector space OurBigBook.com
An affine subspace of a vector space is a translate v+W of a vector subspace W. Its dimension is the dimension of W.

Affine hull (aff(S)=a+span{s−a:s∈S})

Words: 66
Affine subspace OurBigBook.com
The smallest affine subspace containing a nonempty set S. For any chosen a∈S, the displayed formula proves existence and minimality: every containing affine subspace must contain all the indicated differences in its direction space. Equivalently it consists of finite affine combinations ∑i​λi​si​ with ∑i​λi​=1. Its dimension can be smaller than the dimension of an affine hyperplane in which the set has been embedded.

Affine hyperplane (H={v∈V:ℓ(v)=c},ℓ=0)

Words: 68
Affine subspace OurBigBook.com
In a finite-dimensional real vector space, a level set of a nonzero linear functional is an affine hyperplane. Choosing v0​ in that level set gives H=v0​+kerℓ, so its dimension is one less than that of the ambient space. With a Euclidean inner product, translation followed by an orthonormal basis of kerℓ identifies it isometrically with the lower-dimensional Euclidean space. The coordinate-sum constraint on balanced cut vectors is an example.

Affine line in a vector space (a+kv={a+tv:t∈k},v=0)

Words: 56
Affine subspace OurBigBook.com
In a vector space over a field k, an affine line is a translate of a one-dimensional vector subspace. Its direction is that vector subspace, so multiplying v by a nonzero scalar preserves the direction. Over a finite field of size q it contains exactly q distinct points. This usage concerns affine subsets of vector spaces, rather than the affine line as an affine scheme.

Linear combination (∑i=1n​ai​vi​)

Words: 316 Articles: 2
Vector space OurBigBook.com
Let V be a vector space over a specified field F, and let v1​,…,vn​∈V. A linear combination is a finite sum
w=∑i=1n​ai​vi​,ai​∈F.
(4)
The coefficients ai​ are scalars from that same field; each term uses scalar multiplication, and the terms are joined by vector addition. For coefficients in the real numbers, negative values reverse arrows and fractional values scale them by fractional amounts. The collection of attainable vectors is the linear span. The column picture in Strang's MIT notes interprets solving a linear system as choosing coefficients to reach a target vector.[ref]
For a concrete calculation over the real numbers, take
v1​=(1,1),v2​=(1,−1),w=(3,1).
(5)
Then 2v1​+v2​=(2,2)+(1,−1)=(3,1)=w. More generally, solving a+b=x and a−b=y gives
(x,y)=2x+y​v1​+2x−y​v2​.
(6)
Every vector in the Euclidean plane is therefore a linear combination of v1​,v2​, so their linear span is all of R2. The target (3,1) has coefficients (2,1); the target (0,2) has coefficients (1,−1), since (1,1)−(1,−1)=(0,2). The displayed formula also makes the coefficients unique. Consequently (v1​,v2​) is an ordered basis, with coordinate vector [(x,y)](v1​,v2​)​=((x+y)/2,(x−y)/2)T.
The payoff is a reusable language for synthesis: linear combinations build vectors from chosen ingredients, linear span decides which targets are reachable, and linear independence decides whether the coefficients are unique. The ingredients can also be polynomials or functions, as long as they belong to a vector space over the specified field.

Thus R2 has dimension two even with an oblique basis, R[x]≤2​ has dimension three, and the homogeneous plane in vector subspace has dimension two. This count concerns independent freedom, so an embedded plane remains two-dimensional while sitting in a three-dimensional ambient vector space. Dimension also depends on the field, as the two interpretations of C in vector space illustrate.

Vector space OurBigBook.com
In a vector space V over a specified field F, a finite family of vectors (v1​,…,vn​) is linearly independent when, for coefficients ai​∈F,
∑i=1n​ai​vi​=0⟺a1​=⋯=an​=0.
(8)
Here the left-hand zero is the zero vector, while the right-hand zeros belong to the field F. Thus linear independence excludes every nontrivial linear relation. For an infinite family, require this condition for every finite subfamily.[ref]
For v1​=(1,1) and v2​=(1,−1) over the real numbers, the linear relation av1​+bv2​=0 gives a+b=0 and a−b=0. Adding and subtracting yields 2a=2b=0, hence a=b=0. This verifies linear independence directly and explains why the linear combination giving (3,1) has exactly the coefficients (2,1).
A linearly independent family cannot contain the zero vector: a coefficient of 1 on that entry and 0 on every other entry would be a nontrivial linear relation. The empty family is linearly independent, because its empty sum is the zero vector and there are no coefficients that could be nonzero. Linear independence identifies a collection without redundant vectors; combined with a spanning set, it gives a basis. The uniqueness of linear combination coefficients makes its representations unambiguous.

Linear independence OurBigBook.com
A family is linearly independent if and only if every vector in its linear span has unique coefficients as a linear combination of that family. For a short proof, subtract two representations to get ∑i​(ai​−bi​)vi​=0; linear independence forces each difference to vanish. Conversely, uniqueness applied to the zero vector forces every linear relation to use only zero coefficients. This explains the practical role of linear independence: a coordinate vector relative to an ordered basis is unambiguous.

The sum supplies a nonzero dependence. If the sum vector is omitted, the remaining vectors are a coordinate basis; if ej​ is omitted, its coordinate in any proposed relation forces the coefficient of the sum vector to vanish, then all other coefficients vanish. Strang's notes illustrate redundant columns by expressing one as the sum of two others.[ref]

For solving a linear system, these alternatives matter; for assigning unique coordinate vectors, one instead chooses a basis.
The following example shows why linear independence depends on the scalar field.

Gilbert Strang's MIT lecture on independence, basis and dimension develops this connection between attainable columns, redundant columns and coordinates.[ref]

Vector space OurBigBook.com
A vector is an element of a vector space. Its defining operations are vector addition and scalar multiplication. An arrow in a Euclidean space is one example; a polynomial or a function can also be a vector when the chosen vector space uses the corresponding addition and scalar multiplication.
For instance, the polynomials p(x)=1+x and q(x)=x−x2 belong to the real vector space of polynomials of degree at most two. Their vector addition gives (p+q)(x)=1+2x−x2, and scalar multiplication gives (2p)(x)=2+2x. In the monomial basis (1,x,x2) these are the coordinate vectors (1,1,0), (0,1,−1), (1,2,−1) and (2,2,0) respectively. The vectors are the polynomials; these tuples are their representations in a chosen basis.
A general vector space does not itself prescribe lengths or angles. A norm supplies a size, while an inner product also supplies angle information and orthogonality. The familiar arrow geometry below belongs to Euclidean vectors, where this extra structure is available.

Vector OurBigBook.com
A Euclidean vector is a vector in a finite-dimensional real inner product space. Choosing an orthonormal basis identifies it with its real vector components in Rn. A geometric arrow represents a Euclidean vector by a length and a direction; translating the arrow without changing either represents the same Euclidean vector. The zero vector has length zero and no distinguished direction.[ref]
For points P=(1,1) and Q=(4,5) in a Cartesian coordinate system, the displacement is Q−P=(3,4). The arrow from (−2,0) to (1,4) represents the same Euclidean vector, even though its endpoints differ. An endpoint is a position; their difference is a vector. In an orthonormal basis (e1​,e2​),
v=(3,4)=3e1​+4e2​,∥v∥2​=32+42​=5.
(13)

Vector addition is componentwise. With u=(2,1) and w=(1,3),
u+w=(3,4).

Geometrically, translate the second arrow so its tail starts at the first arrow's head. The vector sum joins the starting point to the final endpoint. Reversing the order gives the other route around the same parallelogram, so vector addition is commutative. This is the useful bookkeeping behind adding successive displacements, velocities, or forces: direction information survives the calculation. For a force, the Euclidean vector alone does not specify its point of application, which also affects the torque.[ref]
The magnitude of a vector sum is generally different from the sum of the magnitudes. Here ∥u+w∥2​=5, whereas ∥u∥2​+∥w∥2​=5​+10​>5. The triangle inequality explains why the direct displacement cannot exceed the length of this two-segment route. A return displacement (−3,−4) makes the net vector sum zero, although the lengths of the three travelled segments sum to a positive number.
The dot product exposes direction quantitatively: for nonzero Euclidean vectors, ⟨u,w⟩=∥u∥2​∥w∥2​cosθ. For the displayed pair, the dot product is 2⋅1+1⋅3=5, so cosθ=1/2​ and the angle is 45∘. For orthogonal vectors, that dot product is zero. Dividing by magnitudes separates direction from size, which is the purpose of vector normalization.

Birkhoff-von Neumann theorem OurBigBook.com
For a doubly stochastic matrix with a fractional entry, form the row-column bipartite graph of entries strictly between zero and one. Every incident vertex has degree at least two, so there is an even cycle. A matrix supported on that cycle with alternating entries +1,−1 has zero row and column sums. A sufficiently small positive multiple can be both added and subtracted while preserving entry bounds. The original matrix is then the midpoint of two distinct doubly stochastic matrices, so it is not an extreme point.

Irreducible nonnegative matrix
Words: 102 Articles: 1
Nonnegative matrix OurBigBook.com
A square nonnegative matrix A is irreducible if for each pair (i,j) there is an integer k≥0 with (Ak)ij​>0. This says that every index can reach every other through positive entries. The Perron–Frobenius theorem then gives a positive leading eigenvector and an algebraically simple eigenvalue. Irreducibility alone permits other eigenvalues of the same modulus: the cyclic permutation matrix (01​10​) has eigenvalues 1,−1.
Primitive nonnegative matrix
Words: 47
Irreducible nonnegative matrix OurBigBook.com
A square nonnegative matrix A is primitive if some positive integer power Ak has strictly positive entries. It is therefore an irreducible nonnegative matrix. The Perron–Frobenius theorem gives a leading eigenvalue whose modulus is strictly larger than that of every other eigenvalue. Every strictly positive matrix is primitive; the two-cycle permutation matrix is irreducible but not primitive.
Perron–Frobenius theorem (∣λj​∣<λ1​(j>1))
Words: 123
Nonnegative matrix OurBigBook.com
The strictly positive case states that a real square matrix W with Wij​>0 has a positive simple eigenvalue λ and positive left and right eigenvectors, with all other eigenvalues strictly smaller in modulus. The Brouwer fixed-point theorem applied to v↦Wv/(1TWv) on the nonnegative unit simplex gives v>0 and Wv=λv. For another eigenvector z, maximize ∣zi​∣/vi​; the triangle inequality gives ∣μ∣≤λ. Equality forces every modulus ratio and complex argument to agree because every entry is positive, so z is proportional to v and μ=λ. Apply the same argument to WT for a positive left eigenvector; its positive pairing with v rules out a generalized eigenvector at λ, establishing algebraic simplicity. For merely nonnegative matrices a nonnegative leading eigenvector exists. An irreducible nonnegative matrix has a positive leading eigenvector and simple Perron eigenvalue; a primitive nonnegative matrix has the strict modulus gap.

Matrix decomposition

Words: 229
Matrix OurBigBook.com
A matrix decomposition expresses a matrix as a matrix product of factors with simpler structure. An LU decomposition uses triangular factors, a QR decomposition uses an orthogonal matrix and a triangular factor, and a singular value decomposition separates input directions, stretching factors and output directions. The factorization is an identity; the chosen structure determines what it helps compute.
For an original two-by-two example,
M=(21​13​)=(11/2​01​)(20​05/2​)(10​1/21​).
(30)
The outer factors are a lower triangular matrix and an upper triangular matrix, each with unit diagonal as in a unit triangular matrix; the middle factor is a diagonal matrix. Their matrix product is M, and the final diagonal entry 5/2 is the Schur complement of the first entry 2. This is the scalar version of the factorization under block elimination.
To solve Mz=(3,4)T, solve with the three factors in their displayed order from left to right: first the lower triangular factor, then the diagonal factor, then the upper triangular factor. The intermediate vectors are (3,5/2)T and (3/2,1)T, giving the concise answer z=(1,1)T. A new right-hand side uses the same factors. This is why Reusing LU factors for multiple right-hand sides is useful: factorization records work that otherwise would be repeated, while forward substitution and back substitution apply it cheaply.[ref]
Different decompositions reveal different features. A Cholesky decomposition uses positive definiteness of a symmetric matrix, while a singular value decomposition also applies to rectangular matrices and exposes matrix rank. The existence and numerical behaviour of the factors depend on their own hypotheses; for example, an unpivoted LU decomposition can fail when a chosen pivot element is zero even though the matrix is an invertible matrix.

Matrix rank (rankA)

Words: 1k Articles: 8
Matrix OurBigBook.com
The matrix rank of an m×n matrix A over a field F is the dimension of its column space, equivalently the dimension of its row space. It counts linearly independent column directions, with 0≤rankA≤min(m,n). Counting nonzero matrix entries gives a different quantity: an all-ones matrix can have arbitrarily many nonzero matrix entries and still have matrix rank one.[ref]
Consider the following matrix over the real numbers, with columns written as vectors:
A=​121​241​362​​,c1​=​121​​,c2​=​241​​,c3​=​362​​=c1​+c2​.
(34)
The vectors c1​,c2​ are linearly independent: αc1​+βc2​=0 requires both α+2β=0 and α+β=0, so β=α=0. The third column adds no new direction to their linear span, hence rankA=2 despite all nine matrix entries being nonzero. The second row likewise repeats twice the first row.
The column space is a plane through the origin:
colA=span{c1​,c2​}=⎩⎨⎧​​u2uv​​:u,v∈R⎭⎬⎫​.
(35)
Every output has second coordinate twice its first coordinate. Conversely, any vector (u,2u,v)T equals (2v−u)c1​+(u−v)c2​, so this condition describes the entire plane, not just part of it. For example, b=(1,2,0)T=−c1​+c2​ is attainable, whereas b′=(1,3,0)T lies outside the plane.
Elementary row operations expose the same count algebraically. Apply R2​←R2​−2R1​ and R3​←R3​−R1​, interchange the last two rows, multiply the second row by −1, and subtract twice the second row from the first. The resulting reduced row echelon form is
R=​100​010​110​​.
(36)
There are two pivot columns, so the matrix rank is two. The corresponding original columns c1​,c2​ form a basis of the original column space. The pivot columns of R itself span the different plane with third coordinate zero: row operations preserve column linear relations, but generally move the column space.[ref]
Solving the homogeneous linear system Rx=0 gives x1​+x3​=0 and x2​+x3​=0. Taking the free variable x3​=t gives
kerA=span{(−1,−1,1)T},rankA+dimkerA=2+1=3.
(37)
The kernel is the input direction that trades one unit of each of the first two columns for one unit of the third. This trade leaves the output unchanged. The rank-nullity theorem expresses the general balance: for an m×n matrix of matrix rank r, the nullity is n−r. The column space describes reachable outputs; the kernel describes invisible changes to inputs.[ref]
For the attainable output b, one solution is x0​=(−1,1,0)T. Every solution lies in the affine solution space of a linear equation
x=x0​+t(−1,−1,1)T=​−1−t1−tt​​,t∈R.
(38)
Indeed, Ax0​=b and A(−1,−1,1)T=0. Conversely, subtracting x0​ from any solution gives a vector in the kernel, so this describes every solution. For b′, the same row operations on the augmented matrix expose 0=1: the second requirement demands 3 where twice the first requires 2.
In general, a linear system Ax=b is solvable exactly when appending b leaves the matrix rank unchanged:
rank[A∣b]=rankA.
(39)
Appending a vector outside the column space adds an independent direction. When a solution x0​ exists, every solution is x0​+kerA, because A(x−x0​)=0. Thus one count predicts both how many output directions are reachable and, through the rank-nullity theorem, how many independent input directions remain free.[ref]

Matrix rank OurBigBook.com
The column rank of a matrix is the dimension of its image of a linear map, equivalently the dimension of the linear span of its columns. Multiplication on the left by an invertible matrix preserves all column linear relations, and elementary column operations preserve their linear span. Column rank OurBigBook.com
A pivot column of a matrix is a column whose position contains a leading nonzero matrix entry in its row echelon form. The corresponding columns of the original matrix form a basis of its column space. The column positions survive row operations, although the column vectors themselves generally change.[ref]
Row rank (dimrow(A))
Words: 116
Matrix rank OurBigBook.com
The row rank of a matrix is the dimension of the vector space spanned by its rows. Elementary row operations preserve this row space; multiplication on the right by an invertible matrix preserves all linear relations among the rows.
To see why row rank equals column rank, write a reduced row echelon form as R=EA, where E is a product of elementary matrices and is an invertible matrix. Reversibility of the row operations gives equal row spaces for R and A. Also Rz=0 if and only if Az=0, so the columns have exactly the same linear relations. If R has r nonzero rows, its pivot columns are the first r standard basis vectors of Fm and span its column space. Its nonzero rows are linearly independent, since their matrix entries in the pivot positions form an identity matrix. Both dimensions therefore equal r, and both counts transfer back to A.

Two rectangular matrices are related by invertible left and right multiplication exactly when their ranks agree. The rank-r orbit in Matb×a​(k) has dimension r(a+b−r): choose its image in a Grassmannian, then a surjective map to that image. These are the representation orbits of the one-arrow quiver.

Matrix rank OurBigBook.com
The image of the linear map A+B is contained in the sum of the images of A and B. Since the dimension of a vector space of this sum is at most the sum of their dimensions, matrix rank is subadditive. Iteration shows that a sum of r matrices of matrix rank at most one has matrix rank at most r, over any field.
Full column rank (rankA=n)

Matrix rank OurBigBook.com
An m×n matrix has full column rank when its matrix rank is n, equivalently when its columns are linearly independent vectors. This requires n≤m. Its kernel is {0}, so the represented linear map is injective and every solvable linear system Ax=b has a unique solution. It need not reach every output.[ref]
For example,
B=​101​011​​
(40)
has full column rank two, but its column space is the plane b3​=b1​+b2​ in R3. An attainable output fixes the input uniquely as (b1​,b2​)T; an output outside this plane has no preimage.
Full row rank (rankA=m)
Words: 126
Matrix rank OurBigBook.com
An m×n matrix has full row rank when its matrix rank is m, equivalently when its rows are linearly independent vectors. This requires m≤n. Its column space is all of Fm, so the represented linear map is surjective and every linear system Ax=b is solvable. If n>m, its nullity is n−m>0, so solutions are not unique.[ref]
For example, the matrix transpose of the matrix in full column rank is
BT=(10​01​11​).
(41)
It has full row rank two. Every output (p,q)T has solutions (p−t,q−t,t)T, with t∈R. A square matrix of size n has full row rank and full column rank together exactly when its matrix rank is n; then it is an invertible matrix. A nonsquare matrix cannot have both properties, and has no two-sided inverse: such an inverse would make its linear map a linear isomorphism between vector spaces of different dimensions.
